articles.title: How Australia combines modern tech and Indigenous knowledge to fight wildfires
articles.summary: As Europe faces its worst wildfires in decades, Australia offers lessons in disaster preparedness.
articles.content:
The wildfires currently ravaging Europe feel close to home for Professor Marta Yebra, despite being on the other side of the world.

Originally from Spain, the Canberra-based bushfire expert has spent years developing ways for Australia - home to some of the most fire-prone landscapes in the world - to battle its own blazes.

She heads up the Bushfire Research Centre of Excellence, which was set up in the aftermath of Australia's worst fire season on record: the Black Summer fires of 2019-20, which razed a combined area about the size of the UK.

Her team looks at how technology such as satellites, drones and AI can be used to better detect fires, alongside the knowledge of experienced firefighters.

Equally important, though, is the knowledge and experience that has accrued in Australia over thousands of years, and has been passed down through generations.

This is where Australia has an advantage.

The use of fire has been part of the country's Indigenous culture since long before Europeans arrived in the 18th century - but the value of this ingrained knowledge has only been truly realised in recent years.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights Australia's integration of modern technology and Indigenous knowledge to improve wildfire detection and management, offering a meaningful and scalable approach to disaster preparedness with broad environmental and societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: Australia blends technology and Indigenous wisdom to fight wildfires
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Australia faces some of the most dangerous wildfires in the world. After the devastating Black Summer fires in 2019-2020, experts have worked hard to find better ways to detect and manage fires.

**What happened** – Professor Marta Yebra, who leads the Bushfire Research Centre of Excellence in Canberra, combines modern tools like satellites, drones, and artificial intelligence with the knowledge of experienced firefighters. Importantly, her team also uses Indigenous fire management practices that have been passed down for thousands of years.

**Impact** – This approach is unique because it mixes new technology with ancient wisdom. Indigenous Australians have long used fire carefully to protect the land, a skill that was often overlooked before. Now, their knowledge helps improve how fires are detected and controlled, making fire management more effective.

**What's next step** – The Bushfire Research Centre plans to keep developing these combined methods. Their work could help other countries, like those in Europe currently struggling with wildfires, learn how to better prepare and respond to fire disasters.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Australia is improving wildfire safety by combining high-tech tools with Indigenous fire knowledge, creating smarter ways to protect people and nature.

articles.title: Beaver dams 'helping boost drought resilience'
articles.summary: Research shows beavers are creating more wetland areas since being reintroduced to the wild.
articles.content:
Beavers, often described as "ecosystem engineers", were once widespread in Britain but were hunted to extinction about 400 years ago.

In 2015, the semi-aquatic mammals were reintroduced to the wild in the River Otter, Devon, and in February this year four pairs were released to Par and Fowey rivers in Cornwall.

Puttock said: "One of the biggest modifications beavers do is build dams… that creates these really complex wetlands, which for beavers provides them with safety from predators and ability to move around in the landscape.

"Increasingly, our research has shown this provides benefits to us as people and society, building a more resilient landscape."

He said when the landscape holds more water, it built resilience for both flooding and dry periods.

The slow release of water creates both habitat refuge and water resilience, he added.

Puttock said wetland ponds held about 1,000 cubic metres of water each, reducing peak flows by 30% by retaining it in leaky dams.

"One beaver wetland won't solve all of our drought problems," he said.

"But overall, as beavers expand in our landscapes, and also as we do other nature-based solutions or wetland creation schemes... it does mean that we are less prone to droughts."

Puttock said when he started researching beavers a decade ago he was not thinking about wildfires but flood management.

"We're famously a wet country but there's been a whole raft of really positive research coming out of the States that's basically working on the premise that water doesn't burn," he said.

"When we can create wetlands and beaver wetlands, it creates resilient landscapes to drought but also to the extremes of drought such as wildfires.

"Having these wet landscapes can provide that firebreak."

articles.personality_title: Beavers help create wetlands that protect against drought and floods

**Impact** – The wetlands made by beavers do more than just help the animals. They slow down water flow, which keeps water available during dry times and lowers flood risks during heavy rain. These wet areas can also act as firebreaks, helping to stop wildfires from spreading.

articles.title: Superheated magma may power towering lava fountains
articles.summary: Scientists studying magma from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma have discovered that extreme heat can dramatically change how an eruption unfolds. When magma becomes superheated, it can dissolve the tiny crystal seeds that normally trigger crystallization, allowing the molten rock to remain fluid far longer as it rises.
articles.content:
Scientists have identified a heat-driven process inside magma that could help explain why volcanoes with similar characteristics sometimes erupt in very different ways.

An international research team led by The University of Manchester analyzed magma from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma, Spain. The scientists found that "superheating," which occurs when magma becomes hotter than the temperature at which crystals remain stable, can postpone crystal formation as the magma moves toward the surface.

Superheating Removes Crystal Seeds

The study, published in Nature Communications, found that intense heat can dissolve tiny existing crystals that normally act as "seeds" for the growth of new crystals.

Superheating also reorganizes the magma at a microscopic level, making its internal structure more uniform and less favorable for new crystals to develop. These changes can affect both the speed at which magma rises and the ease with which volcanic gases escape. Together, those factors can strongly influence whether an eruption produces dramatic lava fountains or a slower release of lava.

The results provide new insight into a long-running scientific question about how magma's temperature history affects crystallization before and during an eruption.

Lead author, Dr. Barbara Bonechi, Research Associate at The University of Manchester, said: "The history of crystal and bubble growth can dramatically control how a magma erupts; in particular, as more crystals grow, they eventually have a dramatic effect on magma viscosity. Until now, we did not fully understand the dynamics of crystal growth for magmas that received an injection of superheat just before ascent. But using our exciting and newly developed X-ray transparent pressure vessel combined with synchrotron X-ray microtomography, we can actually observe these processes 'in situ'."

Recreating Volcanic Conditions in the Laboratory

To investigate the process, the researchers recreated conditions found inside a volcano using magma collected from the Tajogaite eruption. That magma may have been superheated before the eruption and while it was rising through the crust.

At Diamond Light Source, the team used synchrotron X-ray microtomography to watch crystals form inside the magma in real time. They also conducted complementary ex-situ experiments in Prague, which made it possible to observe the samples over longer periods.

Together, the experiments allowed the scientists to follow crystallization under carefully controlled conditions of intense heat and pressure.

Crystal Growth Delayed for More Than Eight Hours

The difference between the samples was striking. Magma that had not been superheated began forming crystals after about 20 minutes.

By comparison, strong superheating prevented crystal formation for more than eight hours.

The researchers used these experimentally measured nucleation delays in numerical models of magma ascent. These simulations were designed to show how magma moves and changes as it travels upward through Earth's crust.

How Heat Can Change an Eruption

The models indicated that a long delay in crystallization can keep magma relatively fluid, allowing it to rise rapidly toward the surface. This fast-moving magma could help generate dramatic lava fountains.

When crystals begin forming earlier, however, the magma becomes thicker and more viscous. It then rises more slowly, giving volcanic gases additional time to escape and making a gentler, effusive eruption more likely.

The researchers say this newly recognized role of superheating could help volcanologists better interpret monitoring data and improve forecasts of eruption behavior.

Co-author Dr. Margherita Polacci, Senior Lecturer in Volcanology at The University of Manchester, said: "Current volcanic hazard models typically focus on magma chemistry, gas content and pressure changes. This work suggests that pre-eruptive thermal history and crystallization kinetics may also play an important role in controlling magma ascent and eruptive behavior, with implications for volcanic hazard assessment."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in understanding volcanic eruptions by discovering how superheated magma affects eruption dynamics. This insight has broad implications for volcanic hazard assessment, potentially improving eruption forecasting and public safety. The study is detailed, focused, and involves real-world experimental evidence, making it a meaningful advancement in environmental science and hazard mitigation.
articles.personality_title: Superheated magma helps explain why some volcanoes erupt with towering lava fountains

articles.personality_title_fr: Le magma surchauffé explique les fontaines de lave spectaculaires de certains volcans
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps pourquoi des volcans similaires peuvent avoir des éruptions très différentes. Un facteur important est la façon dont le magma, la roche en fusion à l’intérieur du volcan, change en remontant vers la surface.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de l’Université de Manchester a étudié le magma de l’éruption de Tajogaite en 2021 à La Palma, en Espagne. Ils ont découvert que lorsque le magma est surchauffé—chauffé au-delà de la température où les petits cristaux se forment normalement—ces cristaux disparaissent. Sans ces « graines » de cristaux, la formation de nouveaux cristaux prend beaucoup plus de temps. L’équipe a utilisé des rayons X spéciaux pour observer ce processus en temps réel, en laboratoire et avec des modèles informatiques.

**Impact** – Cette découverte explique pourquoi le magma surchauffé reste plus fluide et remonte plus vite, ce qui peut créer de hautes fontaines de lave lors des éruptions. Quand le magma refroidit et que les cristaux se forment plus tôt, il devient plus épais et remonte lentement, entraînant des coulées de lave plus douces. Comprendre cela aide les scientifiques à prévoir le comportement d’une éruption selon l’histoire thermique du magma.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs souhaitent intégrer ces nouvelles connaissances sur la surchauffe et la croissance des cristaux dans les modèles de risques volcaniques. Cela pourrait améliorer les prévisions d’éruption et aider les populations à mieux se préparer.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les scientifiques ont découvert que le magma surchauffé retarde la formation des cristaux, permettant à la lave de remonter rapidement et de créer des fontaines spectaculaires lors de certaines éruptions volcaniques.
articles.personality_title_es: El magma sobrecalentado explica por qué algunos volcanes lanzan grandes fuentes de lava
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han querido entender por qué volcanes con características similares pueden tener erupciones muy diferentes. Un factor clave es cómo cambia el magma, la roca fundida dentro del volcán, mientras sube hacia la superficie.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de la Universidad de Manchester estudió el magma de la erupción de Tajogaite en 2021 en La Palma, España. Descubrieron que cuando el magma se sobrecalienta—se calienta más allá de la temperatura en que normalmente se forman pequeños cristales—estos cristales desaparecen. Sin estas “semillas” de cristales, la formación de nuevos cristales tarda mucho más. El equipo usó rayos X especiales para observar este proceso en tiempo real, tanto en el laboratorio como con modelos por computadora.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo explica por qué el magma sobrecalentado permanece más líquido y sube más rápido, lo que puede provocar altas fuentes de lava durante las erupciones. Cuando el magma se enfría y los cristales aparecen antes, se vuelve más espeso y sube más despacio, causando flujos de lava más suaves. Entender esto ayuda a los científicos a predecir cómo será una erupción según la historia térmica del magma.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren incluir este nuevo conocimiento sobre el sobrecalentamiento y el crecimiento de cristales en los modelos de riesgo volcánico. Esto podría mejorar la predicción de erupciones y ayudar a las comunidades a prepararse mejor.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los científicos descubrieron que el magma sobrecalentado retrasa la formación de cristales, permitiendo que la lava suba rápido y forme fuentes espectaculares en algunas erupciones volcánicas.

articles.title: Injured peregrine reunion 'brought tears to eyes'
articles.summary: The bird of prey was found injured on the ground but was nursed back to health over a month.
articles.content:
Jon Beresford, one of BAR's founders, said finding a peregrine on the ground was unusual.

"Unlike the vast majority of birds, when they fledge they don't land on the ground, they have short flights from the nest and they go back to the nest.

"So somehow she was found grounded and injured.

"So I suspect during her first trips from the nest flying, she's come a cropper, she's hit something," he said.

It was found the bird was the offspring of a male peregrine successfully treated by BAR last year.

But the shelter did not have the facilities for a young bird to continue to learn to fly, so it was taken to an aviary at Leicestershire Wildlife Hospital.

Beresford said all the effort was worth it when the falcon had recovered.

"It's a privilege not only to treat such a magnificent bird as a peregrine falcon, but also to release her and see her fly again so well."

After hearing "some squawks", she found her parents and siblings.

"It really brought tears to our eyes," said Beresford.
articles.reasoning: The article describes the successful rescue, rehabilitation, and release of an injured peregrine falcon, a significant conservation and wildlife welfare achievement. It highlights the positive impact of wildlife care efforts and the emotional and ecological value of restoring a wild bird to health and freedom, which benefits biodiversity and public awareness.
articles.personality_title: Injured peregrine falcon nursed back to health and reunited with family
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Peregrine falcons are birds of prey known for their speed and flying ability. Young peregrines usually do not land on the ground when learning to fly, so finding one injured on the ground is unusual.

**What happened** – A young peregrine falcon was found injured on the ground, likely after hitting something during its first flights from the nest. The bird was taken to a wildlife shelter called BAR, but since they could not provide the space for the young falcon to practice flying, it was moved to an aviary at Leicestershire Wildlife Hospital. Over more than a month, the falcon was cared for and helped regain its strength.

**Impact** – The successful treatment and release of the falcon is important because it shows how wildlife rescue efforts can save young birds that face dangers early in life. The falcon’s return to flying and reunion with its family was a special moment for the rescuers, showing the emotional connection people have with wildlife and the value of protecting these birds.

**What's next step** – After release, the falcon will continue to live in the wild, using its flying skills to survive. The rescue teams will keep caring for other injured birds and work to raise awareness about protecting wildlife.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A young peregrine falcon was saved from injury, successfully healed, and returned to its family thanks to dedicated wildlife rescue efforts.

articles.personality_title_es: Un halcón peregrino herido es rehabilitado y reunido con su familia
articles.personality_presentation_es:
